claim: Reflexion agents that verbally reflect on task feedback and store reflections in an episodic memory buffer achieve 91% pass@1 on HumanEval, exceeding contemporaneous GPT-4's zero-shot 80%.
stance_target: a blanket claim that iterative LLM self-refinement always degrades outputs
scope_conditions: HumanEval code generation benchmark, 2023, GPT-4-era models
quoted_support: Reflexion achieves a 91% pass@1 accuracy on the HumanEval coding benchmark, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art GPT-4 that achieves 80%.

claim: Reflexion's ablations show the feedback signal's type (scalar vs. free-form language) and source (external vs. internally simulated) affect performance, i.e. not all self-refinement feedback is equivalent, and coding-task success depends on grounding in actual test execution results.
stance_target: the rival hypothesis that 'intrinsic self-correction fails without external verification' and that feedback quality/groundedness, not feedback per se, determines whether refinement helps
scope_conditions: Reflexion ablation studies across sequential decision-making, coding, and reasoning tasks
quoted_support: We also conduct ablation and analysis studies using different feedback signals, feedback incorporation methods, and agent types, and provide insights into how they affect performance.

claim: Reflexion's coding-domain success is grounded in externally verifiable pass/fail signals from actual code execution against test cases, not unaided model self-judgment, distinguishing it mechanistically from a NAS setting where the feedback is a single scalar performance metric on a trained/estimated architecture that a small model may not be able to act on.
stance_target: whether Reflexion is a true counter-example to feedback-degrades-LLM-NAS or merely differs in verification structure and domain
scope_conditions: Reflexion coding-domain results vs. architecture search feedback loops
quoted_support: Reflexion is flexible enough to incorporate various types (scalar values or free-form language) and sources (external or internally simulated) of feedback signals
